title: 11 — Design a News Feed System
html:
11 — Design a News Feed System

The one idea: a feed is a precomputed list of post IDs per user. Build it on write (fan-out to followers' feed caches) for normal users so reads are instant, and on read for celebrities whose follower counts make write fan-out explode. Hydrate IDs into full posts from caches at read time.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Web and mobile; publish a post; see friends' posts on the feed.
  • Order: reverse chronological (simplification — ranking is a later discussion).
  • Up to 5,000 friends; 10M DAU; posts contain text, images, video.

Step 2 — High-level design

Two flows: feed publishing and feed building.

API

POST /v1/me/feed    { content, auth_token }       — publish
GET  /v1/me/feed    { auth_token, cursor }        — retrieve

---
title: News feed — publish and read flows
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph Publish
        U1["User"] --> LB1["LB"] --> WS1["Web servers"]
        WS1 --> PS["Post service"] --> PDB[("Post DB + post cache")]
        WS1 --> FS["Fan-out service"]
        FS --> GDB[("Graph DB<br/>friend lists")]
        FS --> Q["Message queue"] --> FW["Fan-out workers"] --> FC[("News feed cache<br/>user_id → [post_id…]")]
        WS1 --> NS["Notification service"]
    end
    subgraph Read
        U2["User"] --> LB2["LB"] --> WS2["Web servers"] --> NFS["News feed service"]
        NFS --> FC
        NFS --> UC[("User cache")]
        NFS --> PC[("Post cache")]
    end

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Fan-out models

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
When feed is built At publish time At read time
Read latency Very fast (precomputed) Slower (gather + merge)
Write cost O(followers) per post — huge for celebrities O(1)
Wasted work Feeds computed for inactive users None
Freshness Immediate Immediate

Hybrid ✅: push for most users; for accounts above a follower threshold, don't fan out — merge their recent posts into the feed at read time. Also skip fan-out to inactive users.

3.2 Fan-out service steps

  1. Fetch friend/follower IDs from the graph DB.
  2. Filter by settings (muted users, blocked, close friends only).
  3. Enqueue (followerId, postId) batches.
  4. Workers prepend postId into each follower's feed list in cache, trimmed to the latest N (e.g. 500–1,000) — older items come from the DB on deep scroll.

Store only IDs in the feed cache — keeps memory small; content is hydrated separately.

3.3 Feed retrieval

  1. Get [post_id…] from the feed cache (paginate with a cursor, not offset).
  2. Merge in celebrity posts (pull).
  3. Hydrate: posts from post cache, authors from user cache, counts from counter cache.
  4. Return JSON; media URLs point at the CDN.

3.4 Cache architecture — five layers

Layer Contents
News feed Feed ID lists per user
Content Post data; hot posts in a separate hot cache
Social graph Followers / following
Action Liked / replied / shared by me
Counters Like, reply, follower counts

Step 4 — Wrap-up

  • Scaling the DB: vertical vs horizontal, SQL vs NoSQL, primary-replica, consistency models, sharding (posts by post_id, feeds by user_id).
  • Stateless web tier, cache aggressively, multiple DCs.
  • Ranking: replace reverse-chronological with an ML-scored ranking service between retrieval and hydration.
  • Monitoring: QPS at peak, feed refresh latency, fan-out lag (time from post to appearing in feeds).

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Feed cache: Azure Cache for Redis lists or sorted sets (LPUSH + LTRIM, or ZADD with timestamp score + ZREMRANGEBYRANK).
  • Posts: Cosmos DB partitioned by authorId (author timeline) with the change feed triggering fan-out — the change feed is the fan-out queue.
  • Fan-out workers: Azure Functions on the Cosmos DB change feed or Service Bus.
  • Social graph: a relational follows(follower_id, followee_id) table indexed both ways is enough for most scales; Cosmos DB Gremlin API if graph traversal matters.
  • Media: Blob Storage + Front Door; SignalR for "new posts available" nudges.

Review checklist

  • Publish and read flows separated.
  • Push vs pull trade-off; hybrid for celebrities and inactive users.
  • Feed cache stores IDs only, trimmed.
  • Hydration from separate caches.
  • Cursor pagination.
  • Fan-out lag as a monitored metric.
